facts.fact: Harsha was born in 590 CE at Thanesar.
Thanesar lies in present-day Haryana.
The Sanskrit name of Thanesar is Sthanvishvara.
Harsha belonged to the Pushyabhuti dynasty, also called the Vardhana dynasty.
The Pushyabhutis at first ruled only a small kingdom in northern India.
Harsha's father Prabhakarvardhan was the ruler of Thanesar.
Prabhakarvardhan took the title Maharajadhiraja and fought the Hunas.
Harsha's elder brother Rajyavardhan was the crown prince.
Harsha's mother Yashomati, wife of Prabhakarvardhan, immolated herself (sati) on her husband's death.
Harsha ascended the throne of Thanesar at the age of 16.
Harsha's accession in c. 606 CE marks the start of the Harsha era.
Harsha's brother-in-law Grahavarman, the Maukhari king of Kannauj, was assassinated.
Grahavarman was killed by Devagupta, the ruler of Malwa.
Rajyashri was Harsha's sister and Grahavarman's wife.
Harsha rescued Rajyashri in the Vindhya forest just as she was about to commit sati.
Shashanka, king of Gauda (Bengal), killed Rajyavardhan.
Harsha's first campaign was against Shashanka, to avenge his brother and rescue his sister.
Against Shashanka Harsha allied with Bhaskaravarman, king of Kamarupa (Assam).
Shashanka's capital was Karnasuvarna in Bengal.
Shashanka, a Shaiva, is said to have cut down the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.
Harsha united Thanesar and Kannauj and made Kannauj his capital.
Harsha controlled Punjab and central India.
Harsha annexed Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.
Harsha defeated the Vallabhi king of Gujarat.
The Vallabhi king Dhruvasena II became Harsha's ally by marrying his daughter.
The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha.
Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha in 618–619 CE.
The defeat fixed the Narmada River as Harsha's southern boundary.
Pulakeshin II ruled from Vatapi (Badami).
Pulakeshin II's Aihole inscription, composed by Ravikirti, records the victory over Harsha.
The Aihole inscription calls Harsha 'Sakalottarapathanatha' (lord of the whole of the north).
Harsha was also known by the title Siladitya.
Harsha sent an embassy to the Tang emperor of China in 641 CE.
Harsha's Banskhera and Madhuban copper-plate inscriptions are sources for his reign.
The contemporary Pallava kingdom had its capital at Kanchipuram.
The contemporary Pandya kingdom had its capital at Madurai.
The source lists the Chola capital as Thanjavur (it became the Chola capital only in the 9th century).
Kalinga and the Chera kingdom were also contemporaries of Harsha.
The impact of feudalism became more visible from the Harsha period.
Bengal, Kalinga, the Central Provinces, Rajputana and Gujarat were under Harsha's direct control (per the source).
Jalandhar, Kashmir, Kamarupa, Sind and Nepal were feudatory territories (per the source).
Provinces were called Bhuktis and were governed by Governors.
Districts were called Vishayas, under Vishayapatis.
Villages, the smallest units, were run by headmen called Gramikas.
Local councils in villages and towns had only limited powers under the governors.
Large land grants called Agraharas were given to Brahmins and Buddhists.
Land grants gave local landholders the right to collect taxes from their lands.
Holders of land grants could also settle local disputes (judicial decentralisation).
Feudalism meant the landed nobility held land from the king in exchange for military service.
Holding land rights was considered a socially superior position.
Brahmins were the major landlords and enjoyed tax exemptions.
Feudal lords defied orders and withheld taxes, leading to the breakup of the empire into feudatory states.
Paying officers with land grants explains why Harsha issued few coins.
Harsha levied three main taxes: Bhaga, Hiranya and Bali.
Bhaga was the land tax, one-sixth of the produce.
Hiranya was a tax paid in cash by farmers and merchants.
Bali was an additional, oppressive tax.
Royal revenue was divided into four parts.
The four parts were for state affairs, paying ministers and officers, rewarding men of letters, and charity to religious institutions.
25% of the taxes collected went to charity and cultural purposes.
Harsha's army is estimated at 100,000 cavalry, 50,000 infantry and 60,000 elephants.
Harsha was assisted by a Mantri Parishad (Council of Ministers).
The council played a role in the selection of the king and in framing foreign policy.
The prime minister was the most important post in the council.
Avanti was the minister for foreign relations and war.
Simhanada was the Commander-in-Chief.
Kuntala was the chief cavalry officer.
Skandagupta was the chief commandant of the elephant force.
Dirghadhvajas were the royal messengers.
Banu was the keeper of records.
The Mahapratihara was the chief of the palace guard.
Sarvagata was the secret service department.
Criminal law under Harsha was stricter than in the Gupta age.
Mimamsakas were appointed as judges.
Banishment and cutting off limbs (maiming) were common punishments.
Trial by ordeal was in practice.
Life imprisonment was the punishment for plotting against the king.
After Harsha embraced Buddhism the death penalty was replaced by life imprisonment.
Hiuen-Tsang was robbed, showing law and order was not well maintained.
Harsha was a Shaiva (follower of Shiva) till about 631 CE.
Influenced by Rajyashri and Hiuen-Tsang, Harsha embraced Mahayana Buddhism.
Harsha remained a secular ruler who respected all faiths.
At the Prayag assembly images of the Buddha, Surya (the Sun) and Shiva were worshipped on successive days.
Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj (643 CE) in honour of Hiuen-Tsang.
Harsha held a great charity assembly at Prayag every five years.
The Prayag assembly was called the Mahamoksha Parishad.
Hiuen-Tsang attended the sixth quinquennial assembly at Prayag.
Harsha wrote three Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda.
Ratnavali is about princess Ratnavali and King Udayana.
Ratnavali means 'Precious Garland'.
Ratnavali is divided into four acts.
Ratnavali contains a reference to the celebration of Holi.
Nagananda has a Buddhist theme — the self-sacrifice of Jimutavahana.
Banabhatta was a poet in Harsha's court.
Banabhatta is dated 606–647 CE.
Banabhatta wrote the Harshacharita, a biography of Harsha ('Deeds of Harsha').
The Harshacharita is written in ornate Sanskrit prose (the source text calls it verse).
Banabhatta's Kadambari is one of the world's earliest novels.
Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang) was the Chinese pilgrim who visited India in Harsha's reign.
Hiuen-Tsang spent nearly 13 years in India (630–643 CE).
Hiuen-Tsang's account is the Si-Yu-Ki.
Hiuen-Tsang was called the 'prince of pilgrims'.
Hiuen-Tsang collected sacred texts and relics and took them back to China.
Hiuen-Tsang found Buddhism popular only in East India.
Prayag and Kanauj had become important centres while Pataliputra and Vaishali were declining.
Hiuen-Tsang described the Shudras as agriculturists.
Untouchables lived outside the village and announced their arrival.
Butchers, fishermen, dancers and sweepers had to live outside the city.
Hiuen-Tsang recorded four divisions of society: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.
Though caste was rigid there was no social conflict between sections.
Brahmanas and Kshatriyas lived simply, while nobles and priests lived luxuriously.
Hiuen-Tsang found Indians short-tempered but hygienic and honest.
People were encouraged to give up meat.
Indians were mostly vegetarian and rarely used onion and garlic.
Sugar, milk, ghee and rice were common in food.
Fish and mutton were eaten on occasions; beef was forbidden.
People wore colourful cotton and silk clothes; fine weaving had reached perfection.
Men and women wore gold and silver ornaments; merchants wore bracelets and women used cosmetics.
Purdah was not followed by the higher class — Rajyashri did not wear it while hearing Hiuen-Tsang.
Nalanda was the leading university of the time, patronised by Harsha.
Nalanda had been founded by the Gupta king Kumaragupta I.
Harsha granted the revenue of about 100 villages for Nalanda's upkeep.
Education was imparted in monasteries and was religious.
The Vedas were taught orally, not written down.
Sanskrit was the language of the learned.
Learning ran from about 9 to 30 years of age.
Wandering bhikkhus and sadhus were respected for their wisdom.
I-Tsing (671–695 CE) was not a contemporary of Harsha.
I-Tsing studied the Vinaya (rules of discipline) for 5 years; it was his main theme.
I-Tsing was aware of the accounts of Fa-Hien and Hiuen-Tsang.
I-Tsing wrote biographies of eminent monks of Nalanda.
Harsha died in 647 CE.
Harsha left no heir, so his empire broke into smaller kingdoms.
After his death the minister Arunashva usurped the throne and clashed with the Chinese envoy Wang Xuance.
Harsha is remembered as one of the last great rulers of northern India before the Islamic invasions.
Pulakeshin II also made his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana viceroy at Vengi, founding the Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra.
